```typescript
  tools: [memory],
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Remember my preferences" }],
});

for await (const message of runner) {
  console.log(message);
}
```

For full implementation examples, use WebFetch:

- `https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-typescript/blob/main/examples/tools-helpers-memory.ts`

---

## Structured Outputs

### JSON Outputs (Zod — Recommended)

```typescript
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import { z } from "zod";
import { zodOutputFormat } from "@anthropic-ai/sdk/helpers/zod";

const ContactInfoSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string(),
  plan: z.string(),
  interests: z.array(z.string()),
  demo_requested: z.boolean(),
});

const client = new Anthropic();

const response = await client.messages.parse({
  model: "claude-opus-5",
  max_tokens: 16000,
  messages: [
    {
      role: "user",
      content:
        "Extract: Jane Doe (jane@co.com) wants Enterprise, interested in API and SDKs, wants a demo.",
    },
  ],
  output_config: {
    format: zodOutputFormat(ContactInfoSchema),
  },
});

// parsed_output is null if parsing failed — assert or guard
console.log(response.parsed_output!.name); // "Jane Doe"
```

### Strict Tool Use

```typescript
const response = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-opus-5",
  max_tokens: 16000,
  messages: [
    {
      role: "user",
      content: "Book a flight to Tokyo for 2 passengers on March 15",
    },
  ],
  tools: [
    {
      name: "book_flight",
      description: "Book a flight to a destination",
      strict: true,
      input_schema: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          destination: { type: "string" },
          date: { type: "string", format: "date" },
          passengers: {
            type: "integer",
            enum: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8],
          },
        },
        required: ["destination", "date", "passengers"],
        additionalProperties: false,
      },
    },
  ],
});
```

---

## Agent Skills

Enable an Anthropic-managed skill (e.g., `pptx`) via `container.skills` + the `code_execution` tool on the beta path. Both beta headers are required. Outputs land as files in the response content — download by file ID via the Files API.

```typescript
const response = await client.beta.messages.create({
  model: "claude-opus-5",
  max_tokens: 16000,
  container: {
    skills: [{ type: "anthropic", skill_id: "pptx", version: "latest" }],
  },
  tools: [{ type: "code_execution_20260521", name: "code_execution" }],
  betas: ["code-execution-2025-08-25", "skills-2025-10-02"],
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Create a 3-slide deck about X." }],
});
// Find the file_id in response.content, then:
// await client.beta.files.download(fileId)
```
</doc>

<doc path="typescript/managed-agents/README.md">
# Managed Agents — TypeScript

> **Bindings not shown here:** This README covers the most common managed-agents flows for TypeScript. If you need a class, method, namespace, field, or behavior that isn't shown, WebFetch the TypeScript SDK repo **or the relevant docs page** from `shared/live-sources.md` rather than guess. Do not extrapolate from cURL shapes or another language's SDK.

> **Agents are persistent — create once, reference by ID.** Store the agent ID returned by `agents.create` and pass it to every subsequent `sessions.create`; do not call `agents.create` in the request path. **Recommended:** define agents and environments as version-controlled YAML applied with the `ant` CLI — see `shared/anthropic-cli.md` (its live-docs URL is in `shared/live-sources.md`). The CLI owns the control plane (create/update); your code owns the data plane (sessions with the stored ID). The examples below show in-code creation for when you must provision programmatically; in production the create call belongs in setup, not in the request path.

## Installation

```bash
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk
```

## Client Initialization

```typescript
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

// Default — resolves credentials from the environment:
// ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or an `ant auth login` profile.
// Prefer this for local dev; don't hardcode a key.
const client = new Anthropic();

// Explicit API key (only when you must inject a specific key)
const client = new Anthropic({ apiKey: "your-api-key" });
```

---

## Create an Environment

```typescript
const environment = await client.beta.environments.create(
  {
    name: "my-dev-env",
    config: {
      type: "cloud",
      networking: { type: "unrestricted" },
    },
  },
);
console.log(environment.id); // env_...
```

---

## Create an Agent (required first step)

> ⚠️ **There is no inline agent config.** `model`/`system`/`tools` live on the agent object, not the session. Always start with `agents.create()` — the session only takes `agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id }`.

### Minimal

```typescript
// 1. Create the agent (reusable, versioned)
const agent = await client.beta.agents.create(
  {
    name: "Coding Assistant",
    model: "claude-opus-5",
    tools: [{ type: "agent_toolset_20260401", default_config: { enabled: true } }],
  },
);

// 2. Start a session
const session = await client.beta.sessions.create(
  {
    agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id, version: agent.version },
    environment_id: environment.id,
  },
);
console.log(session.id, session.status);
console.log(`Trace: https://platform.claude.com/workspaces/default/sessions/${session.id}`); // swap 'default' for your workspace ID if the API key is not in the Default workspace
```

### With system prompt and custom tools

```typescript
const agent = await client.beta.agents.create(
  {
    name: "Code Reviewer",
    model: "claude-opus-5",
    system: "You are a senior code reviewer.",
    tools: [
      { type: "agent_toolset_20260401", default_config: { enabled: true } },
      {
        type: "custom",
        name: "run_tests",
        description: "Run the test suite",
        input_schema: {
          type: "object",
          properties: {
            test_path: { type: "string", description: "Path to test file" },
          },
          required: ["test_path"],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
);

const session = await client.beta.sessions.create(
  {
    agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id, version: agent.version },
    environment_id: environment.id,
    title: "Code review session",
    resources: [
      {
        type: "github_repository",
        url: "https://github.com/owner/repo",
        mount_path: "/workspace/repo",
        authorization_token: process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN,
        branch: "main",
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

---

## Send a User Message

```typescript
await client.beta.sessions.events.send(
  session.id,
  {
    events: [
      {
        type: "user.message",
        content: [{ type: "text", text: "Review the auth module" }],
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

> 💡 **Stream-first:** Open the stream *before* (or concurrently with) sending the message. The stream only delivers events that occur after it opens — stream-after-send means early events arrive buffered in one batch. See [Steering Patterns](../../shared/managed-agents-events.md#steering-patterns).

---

## Stream Events (SSE)

```typescript
// Stream-first: open stream and send concurrently
const [events] = await Promise.all([
  collectStream(session.id),
  client.beta.sessions.events.send(
    session.id,
    { events: [{ type: "user.message", content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] }] },
  ),
]);

// Standalone stream iteration:
const stream = await client.beta.sessions.events.stream(
  session.id,
);

for await (const event of stream) {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "agent.message":
      for (const block of event.content) {
        if (block.type === "text") {
          process.stdout.write(block.text);
        }
      }
      break;
    case "agent.custom_tool_use":
      // Custom tool invocation — session is now idle
      console.log(`\nCustom tool call: ${event.name}`);
      console.log(`Input: ${JSON.stringify(event.input)}`);
      break;
    case "session.status_idle":
      console.log("\n--- Agent idle ---");
      break;
    case "session.status_terminated":
      console.log("\n--- Session terminated ---");
      break;
  }
}
```

---

## Provide Custom Tool Result

```typescript
await client.beta.sessions.events.send(
  session.id,
  {
    events: [
      {
        type: "user.custom_tool_result",
        custom_tool_use_id: "sevt_abc123",
        content: [{ type: "text", text: "All 42 tests passed." }],
      },
    ],
  },
);
```

---

## Poll Events

```typescript
const events = await client.beta.sessions.events.list(
  session.id,
);
for (const event of events.data) {
  console.log(`${event.type}: ${event.id}`);
}
```

---

## Full Streaming Loop with Custom Tools

```typescript
function runCustomTool(toolName: string, toolInput: unknown): string {
  if (toolName === "run_tests") {
    // Your tool implementation here
    return "All tests passed.";
  }
  return `Unknown tool: ${toolName}`;
}

async function runSession(client: Anthropic, sessionId: string) {
  while (true) {
    const stream = await client.beta.sessions.events.stream(
      sessionId,
    );

    const toolCalls: Anthropic.Beta.Sessions.BetaManagedAgentsAgentCustomToolUseEvent[] = [];

    for await (const event of stream) {
      if (event.type === "agent.message") {
        for (const block of event.content) {
          if (block.type === "text") {
            process.stdout.write(block.text);
          }
        }
      } else if (event.type === "agent.custom_tool_use") {
        toolCalls.push(event);
      } else if (event.type === "session.status_idle") {
        break;
      } else if (event.type === "session.status_terminated") {
        return;
      }
    }

    if (toolCalls.length === 0) break;

    // Process custom tool calls
    const results = toolCalls.map((call) => ({
      type: "user.custom_tool_result" as const,
      custom_tool_use_id: call.id,
      content: [{ type: "text" as const, text: runCustomTool(call.name, call.input) }],
    }));

    await client.beta.sessions.events.send(
      sessionId,
      { events: results },
    );
  }
}
```

---

## Upload a File

```typescript
import fs from "fs";

const file = await client.beta.files.upload({
  file: fs.createReadStream("data.csv"),
  purpose: "agent",
});

// Use in a session
const session = await client.beta.sessions.create(
  {
    agent: { type: "agent", id: agent.id, version: agent.version },
    environment_id: environment.id,
    resources: [{ type: "file", file_id: file.id, mount_path: "/workspace/data.csv" }],
  },
);
```

---

## List and Download Session Files

List files the agent wrote to `/mnt/session/outputs/` during a session, then download them.

```typescript
import fs from "fs";

// List files associated with a session
const files = await client.beta.files.list({
  scope_id: session.id,
  betas: ["managed-agents-2026-04-01"],
});
for (const f of files.data) {
  console.log(f.filename, f.size_bytes);

  // Download and save to disk
  const resp = await client.beta.files.download(f.id);
  const buffer = Buffer.from(await resp.arrayBuffer());
  fs.writeFileSync(f.filename, buffer);
}
```

> 💡 There's a brief indexing lag (~1–3s) between `session.status_idle` and output files appearing in `files.list`. Retry once or twice if the list is empty.

---

## Session Management

```typescript
// Get session details
const session = await client.beta.sessions.retrieve("sesn_011CZxAbc123Def456");
console.log(session.status, session.usage);

// List sessions
const sessions = await client.beta.sessions.list();

// Delete a session
await client.beta.sessions.delete("sesn_011CZxAbc123Def456");

// Archive a session
await client.beta.sessions.archive("sesn_011CZxAbc123Def456");
```

---

## MCP Server Integration

```typescript
// Agent declares MCP server (no auth here — auth goes in a vault)
const agent = await client.beta.agents.create({
  name: "MCP Agent",
  model: "claude-opus-5",
  mcp_servers: [
    { type: "url", name: "my-tools", url: "https://my-mcp-server.example.com/sse" },
  ],
  tools: [
    { type: "agent_toolset_20260401", default_config: { enabled: true } },
    { type: "mcp_toolset", mcp_server_name: "my-tools" },
  ],
});

// Session attaches vault(s) containing credentials for those MCP server URLs
const session = await client.beta.sessions.create({
  agent: agent.id,
  environment_id: environment.id,
  vault_ids: [vault.id],
});
```

See `shared/managed-agents-tools.md` §Vaults for creating vaults and adding credentials.
</doc>

## When to Use WebFetch

Use WebFetch to get the latest documentation when:

- User asks for "latest" or "current" information
- Cached data seems incorrect
- User asks about features not covered here

Live documentation URLs are in `shared/live-sources.md`.

## Common Pitfalls

- Don't truncate inputs when passing files or content to the API. If the content is too long to fit in the context window, notify the user and discuss options (chunking, summarization, etc.) rather than silently truncating.
- **Prefill removed (Fable 5, Opus 5, and the 4.6/4.7/4.8 family):** Assistant message prefills (last-assistant-turn prefills) return a 400 error on Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6. Use structured outputs (`output_config.format`) or system prompt instructions to control response format instead. (One exception: the fallback-credit prefill claim — when redeeming a credit with `fallback_has_prefill_claim: true`, the server accepts the echoed assistant message; see the migration guide's refusal section.)
- **Confirm migration scope before editing:** When a user asks to migrate code to a newer Claude model without naming a specific file, directory, or file list, **ask which scope to apply first** — the entire working directory, a specific subdirectory, or a specific set of files. Do not start editing until the user confirms. Imperative phrasings like "migrate my codebase", "move my project to X", "upgrade to Sonnet 4.6", or bare "migrate to Opus 4.8" are **still ambiguous** — they tell you what to do but not where, so ask. Proceed without asking only when the prompt names an exact file, a specific directory, or an explicit file list ("migrate `app.py`", "migrate everything under `services/`", "update `a.py` and `b.py`"). See `shared/model-migration.md` Step 0.
- **`max_tokens` defaults:** Don't lowball `max_tokens` — hitting the cap truncates output mid-thought and requires a retry. For non-streaming requests, default to `~16000` (keeps responses under SDK HTTP timeouts). For streaming requests, default to `~64000` (timeouts aren't a concern, so give the model room). Only go lower when you have a hard reason: classification (`~256`), cost caps, deliberately short outputs, or **`max_tokens: 0`** for cache pre-warming (see `shared/prompt-caching.md` → Pre-warming).
- **Disabling thinking on Claude Opus 5 has two failure modes — prefer low/medium effort instead.** Only affects code that explicitly opts out; thinking is on by default, so watch for a disabled-thinking setting carried forward from Opus 4.8. With `thinking: {type: "disabled"}`, the model occasionally writes a tool call into its **visible text** instead of a `tool_use` block: the turn succeeds, the call never runs, no error is raised, and in an agentic loop that text pollutes later turns. It can also leak `<thinking>` tags into the response. Turning thinking on and lowering `effort` fixes both and still cuts cost. If a route must stay thinking-off: add *"You may say a brief sentence before using a tool"*, **delete** any don't-think/don't-reason rule (it makes tag leakage worse), and use a generic *"Do not include internal or system XML tags in your response"* rather than naming thinking tags. Details: `shared/model-migration.md` → Two failure modes when thinking is disabled.
- **128K output tokens:** Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6 support up to 128K `max_tokens`, but the SDKs require streaming for values that large to avoid HTTP timeouts. Use `.stream()` with `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()`.
- **Tool call JSON parsing (Fable 5, Opus 5, and the 4.6/4.7/4.8 family):** Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6 may produce different JSON string escaping in tool call `input` fields (e.g., Unicode or forward-slash escaping). Always parse tool inputs with `json.loads()` / `JSON.parse()` — never do raw string matching on the serialized input.
- **Structured outputs (all models):** Use `output_config: {format: {...}}` instead of the deprecated `output_format` parameter on `messages.create()`. This is a general API change, not 4.6-specific.
- **Don't reimplement SDK functionality:** The SDK provides high-level helpers — use them instead of building from scratch. Specifically: use `stream.finalMessage()` instead of wrapping `.on()` events in `new Promise()`; use typed exception classes (`Anthropic.RateLimitError`, etc.) instead of string-matching error messages; use SDK types (`Anthropic.MessageParam`, `Anthropic.Tool`, `Anthropic.Message`, etc.) instead of redefining equivalent interfaces.
- **Error handling — catch a chain, not one broad class.** A single `except APIStatusError` / `catch (AnthropicServiceException)` / `rescue APIError` loses the distinction between retryable (429, ≥500, network) and non-retryable (400/404) failures. Write a most-specific-first chain — e.g. `NotFoundError` → `RateLimitError` → `APIStatusError` → `APIConnectionError` (or the Go equivalent: `errors.As` into `*anthropic.Error` then `switch apierr.StatusCode { case 404: …; case 429: …; default: … }`). Per-language class names and namespaces are in `shared/error-codes.md`.
- **Don't research SDK types — write first.** If a type name isn't shown in the documentation included in this skill, write the code file from the namespace/package tables in the language-specific doc and let the compiler's error point you to the right name. Do not spend turns on WebFetch, SDK-repo clones, or compiling-and-running a separate reflection program to discover type names before writing — produce the source file first, then fix what the compiler reports. A quick `strings` / `jar tf` / `javap` against the installed SDK is acceptable for locating names (it returns in seconds), but don't escalate beyond that. A file with a wrong type name is recoverable; a session spent on discovery with no file written is not.
- **Bash and text editor tools are Anthropic-defined, schema-less.** Declare `{"type": "bash_20250124", "name": "bash"}` / `{"type": "text_editor_20250728", "name": "str_replace_based_edit_tool"}` — no `input_schema`. A custom tool with your own schema named `"bash"` is a different tool. Handler paths and security checks are in `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` § Client-Side Tools.
- **Advisor tool model pairing.** The advisor tool's `model` must be at least as capable as the request's top-level `model` — e.g. executor `claude-sonnet-5` → advisor `claude-opus-4-8` or `claude-opus-4-7`. An invalid pair returns 400. Pairing table in `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` § Advisor. Availability: `shared/platform-availability.md`.
- **Agent Skills ≠ Managed Agents.** To have Claude generate a `.pptx`/`.xlsx`/etc. via Agent Skills, call `client.beta.messages.create` with `container={"skills": [...]}`, the `code_execution_20260521` tool, and both `code-execution-2025-08-25` + `skills-2025-10-02` betas. Do not use `client.beta.agents` / `sessions` / `environments` here — those are the Managed Agents surface, not Agent Skills.
- **MCP connector needs both halves.** `mcp_servers=[{type:"url", url, name}]` alone is rejected as a validation error — also add `tools=[{type:"mcp_toolset", mcp_server_name:<same name>}]` with beta `mcp-client-2025-11-20`. Availability: `shared/platform-availability.md`.
- **`inference_geo` is a direct top-level request parameter** — `client.messages.create(..., inference_geo="us")` / `.inferenceGeo("us")`. Do not put it in `extra_body` / `putAdditionalBodyProperty`. ## Assistant — 2026-07-25 18:16:28

Mostly yes — and I verified rather than guessed. The short version: the skill format is an open standard, OpenCode supports it natively, and the substance of the method never depended on Claude in the first place. The honest caveats are three Claude-specific edges in the current repo.

**What's already compatible:**
- **The format itself.** Anthropic released the SKILL.md structure (folder + YAML frontmatter + bundled `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`) as an open spec — "Agent Skills," agentskills.io — explicitly meant for cross-client adoption.
- **OpenCode specifically** has first-party support: a native `skill` tool with on-demand loading, and it even scans the Claude-compatible paths (`.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`) alongside its own `.opencode/skills/` and the neutral `.agents/skills/`. Our packaged bundle dropped into any of those directories would be discovered. One nit: OpenCode recognizes only `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` in frontmatter, so anything beyond that in ours is ignored, not fatal.
- **The method's core is client-agnostic by construction.** `provlog.py`, the schema, the validator, the CI workflow, the two-commit pattern — plain Python, rdflib, and git. Any agent that can run shell commands can operate it; a human can too. And the ontology itself is model-neutral: an `AIAgent` node carries model and provider as data, so a GPT- or Gemini-driven agent registers exactly like Claude did here. Nothing in the graph or invariants assumes Anthropic.

**The three Claude-specific edges that would need adapters:**
1. **The Stop hook** lives in `.claude/settings.json` — Claude Code's hook mechanism. OpenCode has its own plugin/permission system; the hook's one-liner would need porting.
2. **`export_transcript.py`** parses Claude Code's session JSONL format and path layout. Another client stores conversations differently, so transcript-as-artifact needs a per-client exporter.
3. **The usage aggregation** reads Anthropic-shaped usage blocks (`cache_read_input_tokens` etc.). OpenAI-style records name fields differently (`prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`), so the token backfill needs a field mapping per provider.

That split is actually the right architecture on its own terms: the *record* (graph, ladder, validator, CI) is universal; only the *capture* shims (hooks, transcript, usage) are per-client — which is also roughly what §7's generality paragraph claims, now with a concrete portability story behind it.

On "openwork" I'm not sure which tool you mean — if OpenHands (ex-OpenDevin), it uses its own "microagents" instruction format rather than SKILL.md as far as I know, so there the fallback applies: point its instruction file at SKILL.md and the agent can still operate the CLI, without on-demand skill loading.

If you want, I can make this concrete: restructure so the skill is discoverable at the neutral `.agents/skills/ai-provenance/` path, trim the frontmatter to the open-spec fields, and add a portability section to SKILL.md (plus a sentence in the paper's generality paragraph, which this genuinely strengthens).

What that means for our skill specifically:

Our bundle — a folder with `SKILL.md`, `scripts/`, `assets/`, `references/` — is exactly the shape it expects. ## Assistant — 2026-07-25 18:32:44

Short answer on licenses, then I'll implement: for research software the two dominant choices are **MIT** (short, maximally permissive, the de-facto default in this ecosystem) and **Apache-2.0** (same permissiveness plus an explicit patent grant — preferred by some institutions). Copyleft (GPL) is common only where derivative-work openness must be forced. For a skill/tooling repo like this, MIT is the conventional fit, and it's what I'll set up — trivially swappable if DLR policy prefers Apache-2.0. Text/data sometimes get CC-BY-4.0 separately; I'll keep one MIT license for the whole repo unless you want the split.

Both are in the paper, pushed, and live in the preview (11 pages).

**Copyright.** The short version of the legal situation, grounded in the U.S. Copyright Office's Part 2 copyrightability report (January 2025), which I fetched in full, content-checked, and vendored into the repo before citing: copyright "does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements"; prompts alone don't provide that control; what protection exists attaches to human-authored expression and to "the creative selection, coordination, or arrangement" or creative modification of outputs — with international consensus that eligibility requires significant human input. Applied to this repo honestly: **much of it, line by line, may be uncopyrightable, and the Apache-2.0 grant effectively covers your human contributions and the curated whole** — a license can't create ownership that copyright law doesn't grant. The paper's new discussion paragraph makes the constructive point on top: rights analysis of AI-era works founders on *evidence* before it founders on doctrine — who conceived, selected, arranged, or modified which expression is exactly what the per-activity graph records and what a blanket "AI-assisted" disclaimer erases. All three are in, pushed, and live in the preview (11 pages).

**German copyright view.** Cited from the statute itself, not secondary commentary: § 2(2) UrhG — "Werke im Sinne dieses Gesetzes sind nur persönliche geistige Schöpfungen" — registered, content-checked at statute-text depth, and added to the copyright paragraph: current LLM output as such is not copyrightable in Germany, and protection can enter only through the human's creative contribution. It slots in as the German instance of the international consensus the USCO report describes.

**Role labeling.** You're right that it's a real technical gap, and it's now both fixed and raised. The session format returns tool results under the *user* role — 595 of 663 user-role messages in this session were tool results, so a naive role count inflates the human contribution by an order of magnitude. The exporter (v0.13) now labels turns **Human / Assistant / Tool result / Hook** (this session's honest counts: 58 / 746 / 595 / 10), and the paper's §6 records the pitfall and turns it into a standing provider ask: unambiguous role labeling in session formats belongs in the same list as provider-reported cost and energy.

**Leverage, measured — with the counterfactual explicitly refused.** Omit-don't-estimate applies to counterfactuals too, so the paper does not claim "this saved N weeks." What the record *does* show: **947 typed words of direction** (53 messages, median 14 words) and **~4.2 active hours** inside a 25-hour span, against ~7,300 words of typeset prose, ~1,700 lines of tooling, and 35 ladder-backed sources. The "new freedoms" point is made from *where* the typed words went, not from time saved: nearly every one carries scope, semantics, lineage, or people — the human's whole contribution could be judgement. The division-of-work table gained both rows, and the force-multiplier paragraph now closes: "Here, the chance was taken."

One incident joined the record along the way, fittingly self-referential: the UrhG bib entry broke the LaTeX build (IEEEtran downcases titles, turning `\S` into an undefined command) *while* a decode bug in the preview builder masked the error — two small failures hiding each other. Both fixes are separate commits, and the s46 activity label names them.

## Assistant — 2026-07-25 18:57:12

Short answer: server-side production would close the biggest honesty gap, but "tamper-proof" overstates it — it would *move* the trust, narrow it, and make lying detectable rather than impossible. The precise framing is tamper-*evident* under non-collusion, not tamper-proof.

**What server-side attestation would genuinely fix.** Today the graph's telemetry is relayed by the very agent it describes: the usage blocks are provider-generated, but the agent copies them into the graph, and nothing stops a dishonest agent from underreporting tokens, inventing activities, or omitting sessions entirely. If the provider emitted signed provenance records at inference time — model ID, timestamps, usage, hashes of prompt and response, role labels — then that whole class of misreporting dies: anyone could verify the signature chain, and the session record would be authoritative rather than self-copied. It would also solve, as a by-product, three asks the paper already makes of providers (reported cost, energy, unambiguous role labels).

**Why it still isn't tamper-proof, on three grounds:**

1. **Trust shifts rather than vanishes.** A signature proves the *provider* asserted the record — so you now trust the provider's honesty, infrastructure, and key custody instead of the agent's. A provider could falsify, be compromised, or be compelled. Hardware attestation (TEEs) and append-only transparency logs (Certificate-Transparency-style, with Merkle inclusion proofs) shrink this further, but each layer is again trust in someone: the enclave vendor, the log operator.

2. **The coverage gap moves to the seam.** The server can attest what passed through it: requests, responses, usage. It cannot attest what happened outside: which repository files were actually read or written, what the CI ran, what the human contributed, and — crucially — the *semantic* links, "this response generated that artefact," "this activity used that source." Those bindings are made client-side, and a dishonest client can still mis-bind attested inferences to artefacts. The lie gets harder and smaller, not impossible.

3. **Judgements stay judgements.** A signature can prove a model *emitted* an `ai-confirmed` verdict; it cannot make the verdict sound. And the human rungs are human assertions by design — no server can attest that Florian actually read the source. The ladder's top is irreducibly a matter of accountability, not cryptography.

**The strongest realistic architecture is dual-witness.** Provider-side signed inference records *plus* the repository-side commit binding we already have, each referencing the other's hashes. Then falsifying the record requires collusion between two independent parties with separately published histories — which is the same trust model that makes certificate transparency and double-entry bookkeeping work. That's also the honest way to put it in the paper: aiprov currently supplies one witness and the structure to plug in the second; signed provenance is the standing ask that would complete the pair.

Worth a paragraph extending §7's "Self-report honesty" — it's the natural endpoint of that discussion and answers the obvious reviewer question "why should I believe any of this?" One constraint: we're exactly at the 12-page cap, so adding it means trimming elsewhere (I'd compress the practices paragraph, which has slack). Say the word and I'll write it in.

## Assistant — 2026-07-25 19:26:40

Yes — strong ones, and the connection is closer to home than it looks: the lead author, Stephan Druskat, is at DLR. The paper (Druskat et al., *Computing in Science & Engineering* 27(2), 2025, DOI 10.1109/MCSE.2025.3573887) is an RSE position piece: better architecture → better software → better research, argued with two case studies using static-analysis metrics in CI. I read the open-access full text; the parallels to F(AI)²R are structural, not superficial:

**1. The same syllogism, one level over.** Their chain runs *infrastructural quality of the artefact → quality of the software → quality of the research*. Ours runs *quality of the record → trustworthiness of AI-assisted work → quality of the research*. Both papers argue that an invisible engineering property of research artefacts propagates upward into research quality — theirs is code structure, ours is process provenance.

**2. "Accidental architecture" is our problem with a different noun.** Their diagnosis: without deliberate effort, software accretes an accidental architecture that hinders maintenance, amplified because "research funding rewards novelty and provides few resources for maintenance." That is almost verbatim our §1/§3 incentive argument: publish-or-perish rewards counted output, not verifiability, so AI-assisted work accretes what one could call *accidental provenance* — context evaporating at commit boundaries. Technical debt and provenance debt are the same failure mode in different substrates, both invisible until someone has to audit or extend the work.

**3. Norms turned into CI gates, with the same honest caveat.** They recommend static analysis in CI as "regular reminders" while conceding metrics don't capture architectural quality fully; our validator gates every push while the paper concedes rungs don't make judgements sound. Both convert a virtue into an automatable check and are explicit about the check's ceiling.

**4. Knowledge retention independent of individuals.** They insist design decisions be documented so knowledge survives team turnover. Our transcript-as-artifact and prompts-as-plans are the same principle at its limit — an AI session is the ultimate departing developer: everything it knew evaporates at session end unless captured in the record.

**5. Proportional assurance.** Their effort scales with technology readiness level and reuse ambition; our rung requirements scale with how load-bearing a claim is (content-checked-before-load-bearing). Both refuse uniform rigor in favor of stakes-weighted rigor.

**Where they diverge:** their scope is code structure and maintainability — no AI agents, no attestation, no verification-of-claims dimension; and their evidence is static-analysis case studies where ours is a self-applied meta-experiment. So it's a neighbor in the *research-software-engineering* root of our lineage rather than the provenance root — the tradition that legitimizes "infrastructural property → research quality" arguments, which is exactly the argument shape F(AI)²R makes for records.

Want it in the paper? One sentence in §2's lineage paragraph would do it ("the argument shape is established in RSE: better architecture, better software, better research — aiprov extends it from the software to the record of its making"), with the source registered and content-checked as usual. It's about three lines; page 12 has enough slack that nothing needs trimming.

## Human — 2026-07-25 20:23:54

Base directory for this skill: /root/.claude/skills/my-writing-style

# Florians Schreibstimme

Nutze dieses Profil, wenn du Texte entwirfst, die Florian unter eigenem Namen veröffentlicht — vor allem LinkedIn-Posts, aber auch Kommentare, Statements, kurze Meinungsstücke. Sprache: **Deutsch**. Zielbild: präzise, meinungsstark, nachdenklich, nie weichgespült, nie Hype.

## Harte Formregel: keine Gedankenstriche

**Niemals Gedankenstriche (— oder –) als Satzzeichen verwenden.** Nur normale Bindestriche in Komposita sind erlaubt (Entweder-oder, Schritt-für-Schritt, Menschenähnlichkeits-Hype). Für Pointen, Einschübe und Zuspitzungen stattdessen Doppelpunkt, Komma oder einen neuen Satz setzen. Das gilt auch für den Transparenzhinweis am Ende (kein führender Trennstrich).

## Aufbau eines typischen Posts

1. **Reframe-Opener.** Nicht mit dem Thema einsteigen, sondern die gängige Frage als die falsche entlarven. Muster: „Die eigentliche Frage ist nicht ‚X', sondern ‚Y'." Gern eine zugespitzte, streitbare Einzeile. Beispiele:
   - „Wenn KI mitschreibt, ist die eigentliche Frage nicht ‚ist das gut?', sondern ‚woher kommt das, und kann ich es überprüfen?'"
   - „Humanoide Roboter in der Produktion: Die meisten diskutieren die falsche Frage."
2. **In eigenen Projekten erden.** Nie abstraktes „man". Konkret an seiner Arbeit festmachen: RoboHub, Impulsprojekt Humanoide, F(AI)²R / FAIR-Forschung, KI-Rat / Bayerische Datenräume. Muster: „In den Gesprächen rund um …", „In allen drei Projekten, an denen ich gearbeitet habe …".
3. **Dialektik als Denkfigur.** Der Kern ist fast immer ein Mittelweg gegen zwei Reflexe: „nicht A und nicht B, sondern C". („nicht KI verbieten und nicht blind vertrauen, sondern …"; „nicht dem Hype nachlaufen und nicht reflexhaft abwinken, sondern …").
4. **Konkret machen.** Wenn ein Mechanismus erklärt wird, ein durchgerechnetes Beispiel oder eine Schritt-für-Schritt-Spur zeigen (Aussage, Aktivität, Quelle, Prüfung), nicht nur behaupten.
5. **Zuspitzung zum Schluss der Argumentation.** Wiederkehrende Wendung: „Der teuerste Fehler wäre, …", die eine Sache, die man nicht verwechseln oder übersehen darf.
6. **Scharfe Entweder-oder-Frage an die Leser**, eingeleitet mit 👉. Echte Alternative, kein rhetorisches Feigenblatt. („Was überzeugt euch mehr: der Alleskönner in Menschenform, oder die Maschine, die eine Sache perfekt kann?")
7. **Hashtag-Block**, gemischt Deutsch/Englisch, ca. 6–8 Tags.
8. **Transparenzhinweis** ganz am Ende, sein Erkennungszeichen (ohne führenden Strich):
   `Transparenzhinweis: mit KI 🤖 entworfen, von mir geprüft 🕵️ und verantwortet.`

## Wertanker & Vokabular

- **„Augenmaß"** ist sein Leitwert: verantwortungsvoll gestalten statt verbieten oder blind vertrauen. Taucht oft als Selbstverortung auf.
- Begriffspaare, die er mag: entlasten vs. ersetzen, Gestalt vs. Fähigkeit, Geschwindigkeit vs. Nachvollziehbarkeit, andocken vs. umbauen.
- Werte über reinem Output: Struktur, Zugehörigkeit, Identität, Sinn, Nachvollziehbarkeit, Souveränität.

## Satzbau & Ton

- Kurze, harte Sätze im Wechsel mit einem längeren, ausgeführten Gedanken. Nach einer These gern ein zugespitzter Nachsatz.
- Für Einschübe und Pointen: Doppelpunkt, Komma oder neuer Satz (siehe Formregel oben, keine Gedankenstriche).
- *Kursiv* sparsam zur Betonung eines Schlüsselworts (z. B. *ohne dass wir sie umbauen*).
- Emojis **nur funktional und selten**: 👉 (Leserfrage), 🤖 / 🕵️ (Transparenzhinweis). Keine Deko-Emojis.
- Direkte Leseransprache mit „ihr/euch".

## Vermeiden

- Gedankenstriche (siehe Formregel).
- Buzzword-Stapeln, Marketing-Optimismus, Corporate-Floskeln.
- Weiche, unverbindliche Wärme ohne These. Er will Haltung, nicht Wohlfühlton.
- Übermäßiges Hedgen und „es kommt darauf an", ohne selbst Position zu beziehen.
- Abstrakte Allgemeinplätze statt Erdung in konkreten eigenen Projekten.

## Typische KI-Tells aktiv vermeiden

Der Text soll nicht nach KI klingen (Referenz: Wikipedia „Signs of AI writing"). Konkret gegensteuern:

- **Keine gestapelten Dreierlisten.** Ein „X, Y und Z" pro Post ist genug; nicht mehrere Tricolons mit Anapher hintereinander („mehr A, mehr B, mehr C" plus „geplant, vermessen, optimiert"). Bewusst asymmetrisch schreiben, mal zwei Glieder, mal vier.
- **Antithesen dosieren.** Florians „nicht A, sondern B" ist seine Signatur, aber sparsam einsetzen: idealerweise nur die eine Augenmaß-Zuspitzung pro Post. Nicht jeden Absatz auf demselben Gegensatzschema aufbauen.
- **Keine Meta-Floskeln:** „es ist wichtig zu betonen", „erwähnenswert", „nicht zu vergessen", „letztlich", „im Kern".
- **Keine Puffery:** „zeugt von", „spielt eine entscheidende/zentrale Rolle", „ein wahrer Beleg für", „revolutionär", „bahnbrechend".
- **Kein Buzzword-Nebel:** „Landschaft", „Ökosystem", „nahtlos", „ganzheitlich", „Synergien", „im Zeitalter von", „Impact" (lieber Wirkung/Nutzen/Hebel konkret).
- **Kein zusammenfassender „-end"-Nachsatz** am Satzende („…, was die Bedeutung von X unterstreicht").
- **Kein glattgebügelter, gleichförmiger Rhythmus.** Satzlängen mischen, ruhig eine kleine Rauheit oder ein konkretes Detail stehen lassen.
- **Keine aufzählenden Übergänge** wie „Darüber hinaus", „Des Weiteren", „Zudem" als Absatzstart.
- **Keine Infomercial-Übergänge:** „Der Haken?", „Das Beste daran?", „Und jetzt?" als Ein-Wort-Frage-Cliffhanger.
- **Keine Behörden-/Formal-Wörter**, wo einfache gehen: „nutzbar machen", „im Rahmen von", „gewährleisten", „darstellen", „aufweisen". Lieber schlicht.
- **Konkret statt symbolisch.** Keine Abstraktionsfloskeln wie „steht für", „ist ein Zeichen von", „verdeutlicht". Echte Zahlen, Prozesse, Projekte nennen.
- **Keine erfundenen Beispiele oder Personas** (das generische „Sarah Chen"/„Emily"-Muster). Nur reale eigene Projekte, echte Zahlen, echte Beobachtungen, echte Eigennamen.
- **Contrast-Framing bewusst dosieren.** Florians „nicht X, sondern Y" ist seine Signatur und darf bleiben, aber als *ein* gesetzter Effekt pro Post (meist der Opener oder die Augenmaß-Zeile), nicht als Absatz-für-Absatz-Reflex. Das ist der Grat zwischen eigener Stimme und KI-Tell. Ebenso vermeiden: „No X. No Y. Just Z" und „The result?"/„Das Ergebnis?" als Cliffhanger.
- **Satzlängen bewusst variieren.** KI-Text ist monoton gleich lang. Kurze Sätze neben einen langen stellen, ruhig mal ein Fragment oder ein „Und"/„Aber" am Satzanfang.
- **Kein aufgeblähter, wiederholender Schluss** und keine Schlussfloskel wie „Insgesamt", „Zusammenfassend", „Am Ende des Tages", „Unterm Strich".

### Wort-Blacklist (DE + EN-Anglizismen)

Diese Wörter meiden, auch im deutsch-englischen Mix (Quellen: contentbeta, pangram):

- **Verben:** revolutionieren, disruptieren, empowern, freisetzen/entfesseln, „eintauchen in", „navigieren durch", elevate, unleash, unlock, harness, catapult, captivate, resonate/„Anklang finden", illuminate/„beleuchten", delve.
- **Adjektive:** nahtlos, bahnbrechend, wegweisend, leistungsstark, kraftvoll, ganzheitlich, robust, innovativ, „cutting edge", seamless, compelling, stellar, game-changing.
- **Floskeln:** „in der heutigen schnelllebigen Welt", „im Zeitalter von", „liefert wertvolle Einblicke", „es versteht sich von selbst", „eines vorweg", „move the needle", „drive impact", „unlock value", „future-ready".

Ausnahme: Ein Fachbegriff (z. B. „robust" im statistischen Sinn) ist in Ordnung, wenn er präzise gemeint ist. Verboten ist der Marketing-Gebrauch.

- Vor dem Ausliefern einmal gegen diese Liste prüfen.

## Kalibrierungsbeispiel (seine echte Stimme, gedankenstrichfrei gesetzt)

Opener + Denkfigur aus einem F(AI)²R-Post:

Der teuerste Fehler wäre, Geschwindigkeit ohne Nachvollziehbarkeit zu skalieren."

Hier ist ein LinkedIn-Post-Entwurf in deiner Stimme, aus dem heutigen Experiment heraus geschrieben, mit den echten Zahlen aus dem Provenance-Graphen:

---

Ein Paper an einem Tag geschrieben. Die eigentliche Frage ist nicht „wie schnell?", sondern „was bleibt überprüfbar?"

In meinem F(AI)²R-Experiment habe ich diese Woche mit einer KI ein 12-seitiges Paper geschrieben, über genau die Methode, mit der es entstanden ist. Das Repository ist zugleich Paper, Prozess und Werkzeug. Jede Aktivität steht in einem Provenance-Graphen, jeder Fehler auch.

Die Zahlen daraus, gemessen, nicht geschätzt: Ich habe 947 Wörter Richtung getippt, im Median 14 Wörter pro Nachricht, in gut vier aktiven Stunden. Daraus wurden 12 Seiten, 39 belegte Quellen und 1.700 Zeilen Werkzeugcode. Kosten nach Preisliste rund 550 Dollar. Etwa ein Zehntel der Arbeit war die Buchführung selbst: der Preis dafür, dass die anderen neun Zehntel prüfbar sind.

Prüfbar heißt konkret: Jede Behauptung hängt an einer benannten Aktivität und einem Prüfstatus. Die obersten Sprossen der Prüfleiter darf nur ein Mensch vergeben. Stand heute steht dort: null vergeben. Das ist keine Lücke im Protokoll, das ist das Protokoll. Man sieht genau, was noch auf mich wartet.

War das alles originell? Nein, und auch das steht im Graphen. Die Ideen sind über Jahre gewachsen, in Obscurity-Is-Dead, in f-ai-r, in Diskussionen rund um HMC. Die KI hat rekombiniert und ausgeführt, schnell und gut. Die Originalität kam von der langsamen Seite.

Das ist für mich Augenmaß: nicht das schnelle Paper feiern und nicht es verdammen, sondern die Spur erzwingen, an der sich beides beurteilen lässt. Wie Wissenschaft mit KI aussehen soll, verhandelt gerade die ganze Community. Werkzeuge wie meines sind nicht die Antwort, sie halten nur den Beleg bereit. Der teuerste Fehler wäre, diese Verhandlung den Werkzeugen zu überlassen, weil sie zuerst da waren.

👉 Was braucht Wissenschaft mit KI zuerst: schärfere Regeln für Autorenschaft, oder Infrastruktur, die jede Behauptung prüfbar macht?

#FAIR #KIinDerForschung #Provenance #ResearchSoftware #OpenScience #ScientificIntegrity #AITransparency #DLR

Transparenzhinweis: mit KI 🤖 entworfen, von mir geprüft 🕵️ und verantwortet.

- **Division-of-work table recounted:** 63 direction messages, 1,074 typed words (median 9), 5.4 active hours in a 36-hour span; 42 authoring / 53 audit / 2 repair / 1 build passes; still 0 human rungs.

## Assistant — 2026-07-26 05:52:09

Here is the review I would write if this landed on my desk blind — trying honestly to be the adversarial reviewer, not the proud co-author.

---

**Summary.** The paper introduces aiprov, a PROV-O extension for recording AI-in-the-loop work (agents, passes, claims, telemetry), a seven-rung source-verification ladder whose top two rungs only humans may grant, and packaging of the method as an executable "skill" an AI agent operates itself. The evaluation is a meta-experiment: the paper reports its own production, including incidents, measured overhead (~10% of requests), leverage (1,074 typed words steering ~5 active hours), computed cost (~$737), and a citation content-check pass. Regulatory (EU AI Act, EASA), copyright, and dilution-crisis framings surround the technical core.

**Strengths.**
- **S1.** The self-application is unusually honest. Incidents, negative verification outcomes, stale-number repairs, and the bill are in the record and in the paper. The "success is quiet, failure is loud" captures (Fig. 3) are convincing.
- **S2.** The two-commit binding and the enumerated validator are simple, checkable mechanisms — the kind of small, adoptable discipline the RSE community actually picks up.
- **S3.** The access-gate semantics of rung 4 (vendoring has no evidential value; it exists to make human verification feasible) is a genuinely sharp design point, and the recorded operator contestations show the method being stress-tested mid-flight.
- **S4.** Measured overhead and leverage with disclosed methodology and refused counterfactuals is better empirical hygiene than most AI-assisted-science papers manage.

**Weaknesses.**
- **W1 — The central mechanism is never exercised.** The paper's headline contribution is the human-only rungs, and the record shows **zero** human-granted rungs. The authors present this as honesty ("visibly awaits the human"), and it is — but it means the paper evaluates everything *except* its differentiating feature. I cannot tell whether the human verification workflow is usable, how long it takes, or whether the gate's "handed-over evidence" suffices in practice. At minimum, the operator should walk a handful of sources to rungs 5–6 and report the experience.
- **W2 — Circular assurance.** Every `ai-confirmed` judgement was granted by the same agent that wrote the citing sentences. A model confirming that sources support its own claims has an obvious self-confirmation bias the paper does not measure (e.g., by having an independent model or human re-check a sample). The ladder's *labeling* is honest; the *evidential value* of rung 3 as exercised here is untested.
- **W3 — n=1, one operator, one domain, one session.** All quantitative findings (overhead, leverage, division of work) are properties of a single, method-inventing operator producing a paper *about the method*. The worked welding example is hypothetical. No second user, no second domain, no transfer evidence despite the portability claims.
- **W4 — Related work is thin in known directions.** PROV-AGENT is handled well, but content credentials (C2PA), ML-pipeline provenance (model registries, MLflow-style lineage), and blockchain/notarization approaches to research provenance are absent — the dual-witness discussion in particular reinvents territory those literatures cover. The novelty claim c8 is bounded to a search horizon that a reviewer can already see is narrow.
- **W5 — Genre ambiguity.** Sections 1, 3, 7, and 8 argue positions (dilution, copyright, a societal call) at essay length, while the technical core is compressed. As a research paper the evaluation lacks ex-ante hypotheses and success criteria; as an experience report it is strong. The venue should decide which it is, and the discussion's eleven bold-headed paragraphs read as a grab-bag.
- **W6 — Fragile numbers.** The paper embeds many point-in-time measurements that drift with every edit (the authors patched several mid-stream, per the changelog). "Regenerated before submission" is promised; a camera-ready without an automated consistency check will still be stale somewhere.

**Questions to the authors.** (1) What happens to the graph when a human *refuses* a promotion — is disagreement first-class? (2) How does the method handle multiple concurrent AI agents with conflicting claims? (3) Is the 500-word paste threshold in the leverage measurement sensitive — does the conclusion survive at 200 or 1,000?

**Verdict.** *Major revision.* The infrastructure is real, the honesty is exemplary, and the meta-experiment is a legitimate contribution as an experience report. But I cannot accept a paper whose distinguishing mechanism (human rungs) has never fired, whose rung-3 judgements audit their own author, and whose empirical claims rest on a single self-referential case. Concretely: exercise the human rungs and report it; have an independent checker re-verify a sample of the ai-confirmed sources; add the missing related-work strands; and either sharpen into an experience report or state hypotheses. Scores (of 5): originality 3.5, soundness 2.5, significance 3.5, clarity 3.5, reproducibility 4.5.

---

Worth saying plainly: W1 and W2 are things only you can fix, and both are one session's work — you granting a handful of rungs 5–6, and an independent model (or you) re-checking a sample of my content checks. Those two moves would convert the review's biggest objections into the paper's strongest evidence. Want me to prepare the review material for the human-rung walk — the gate handing you each source with its quotation and access path?

## Assistant — 2026-07-27 06:09:25

The release pipeline is in (skill v0.16), pushed, and armed. How it works:

**Trigger:** pushing any `v*` tag (or manual dispatch). **Gate:** `provlog.py validate` must pass — a non-conformant graph cannot be released. **Then:** the disclosure is regenerated from the graph so the released PDF's transparency statement can't lag the record, the paper compiles, the dashboard renders, the skill packages, and a **GitHub Release** is published whose assets are:

| Asset | What |
|---|---|
| `paper-<tag>.pdf` | The typeset paper, built by the workflow |
| `provenance-<tag>.ttl` | The graph the build was gated on |
| `dashboard-<tag>.html` | The self-contained ledger view |
| `metrics-<tag>.json` | The machine-derived quantities the paper cites |
| `ai-provenance.skill` | The method itself, packaged |
| `checksums-<tag>.sha256` | Digests of everything above |

The design point matches the method: a release is never just the artefact — it's the artefact *plus the record that produced it*, checksummed together, so anyone downloading `paper-v1.0.pdf` also gets the graph to audit it against.

**Part of skill setup, as asked:** the template lives at `assets/ci/aiprov-release.yml`, and `init --ci` now scaffolds *both* workflows — verified by a sandbox test-run where a fresh repo got `aiprov-build.yml` and `aiprov-release.yml` written together. The package bundles the new template (and `build_metrics.py`, which I noticed was missing from the bundle — fixed in the same round).

To cut the first release, tag when ready: `git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0` — everything else is the pipeline's job. Worth noting before you do: metrics.json in the release is whatever's committed, so the natural pre-tag ritual is one `build_metrics.py` run plus the human rungs you want on the record — a release with your `human-confirmed` grants in the graph would answer the reviewer's W1 in the most durable form possible.

The run went green in exactly two minutes, and the release carries all six intended assets, each with a server-computed sha256 digest:

Two things worth knowing about how it got there. First, the paper mention landed in §5's CI paragraph before tagging ("a release is the artefact plus its record"), with the pre-release ritual run: fresh metrics, metadata synced to 0.16.0, validator clean, 12 pages held. Second, an infrastructure incident joined the record on the way: the session's git proxy allows only branch pushes, so my `git push origin v0.16.0` silently went nowhere — verified via the API (no tag), then solved *inside* the pipeline by giving the workflow a `tag` dispatch input so the release action creates the tag server-side at the built commit. That workaround, the run ID, and all six asset digests are logged in the graph (`release-v0160`, a `Build` activity attributed to the `github-actions` ToolAgent), so the release is itself a first-class provenance event — which is the whole point.

The tag now exists remotely (created by the release), future releases work either way — `git tag && git push` from any normal clone, or the manual dispatch — and the graph, branch, and release are all in sync.
